newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurotunnel set for make-or-break meeting.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel set for make-or-break meeting.

text.p: Eurotunnel shareholders, ranging from small private investors to large U.S. pension funds, are due to vote on a debt deal on Thursday which could decide the fate of the Channel tunnel operator.

Eurotunnel SA/Plc needs shareholder approval for a plan to restructure its 70 billion franc ($11.8 billion) of junior bank debt in a deal which will reduce the current shareholders' stake in the group from 100 to 54.50 percent.
But if shareholders vote against the plan, despite recent calls for them to approve it, the company's operating licence risks being taken over by creditor banks.
On Tuesday, French Transport Minister Jean-Claude Gayssot said it "was in everyone's interest" that Eurotunnel shareholders approve the plan.
Gayssot, a Communist minister, is due to meet Eurotunnel executive chairman Patrick Ponsolle on Wednesday.
Last week the French and British governments said they were willing to consider extending Eurotunnel's operating licence to at least 99 years from the current 65 years.
But in exchange, they want a 25 percent share of profits after 2052, when the current licence expires.
Financial analysts said the prospect of extending the licence was a psychological boost to the 'Yes' camp, even though it would do nothing for the company's financial performance in the next decade.
"It's the first 10 years that count. If it survives the decade, it will survive forever," one London-based transport analyst said recently.

Sophie l'Helias, a lawyer representing many investors, decided to switch to the 'Yes' camp after the governments' statement on a licence extension said they would not be able to stop Eurotunnel's banks taking over the licence and tunnel if the debt deal was rejected.
She said the statement "makes it impossible for FGIS (her proxy holding firm) to vote against the restructuring plan that will be put to the shareholders on July 10."
Northern Cross Investments of the United States, one of her clients with a stake of around three percent in Eurotunnel, had earlier switched from resistance to support.
Shareholders had originally been due to vote on the debt deal -- reached in April -- on June 24 but insufficient votes were represented at the meeting.
On Thursday, a quarter of the votes have to be registered at the meeting to make decisions legally valid.

Eurotunnel has 721,000 small shareholders, of whom around 600,000 are French. The company's equity capital contains 919,553,419 units, with each unit having one voting right and containing one share in Eurotunnel SA and one in Eurotunnel Plc.

Under the latest financial scenario, Eurotunnel expects to make a net profit in 2005 and pay its first dividend in 2006 --- three years later than it had said in the prospectus for a 1994 rights issue.

Eurotunnel's financial difficulties stem from construction costs which topped 10 billion pounds ($16.9 billion), more than twice what was budgeted, while the start of services has been slow but steady.
A fire in the tunnel in November, when a lorry burnt out on a train and damaged a tunnel section, paralysing cargo traffic for months, added to the problems.

Eurotunnel and building consortium TransManche Link (TML) have been engaged in long legal battles over the cost overruns, each blaming the other and both blaming the French and British governments for changing safety regulations during the construction period.

Some analysts say the problems stem from Eurotunnel's corporate history -- the company obtained its first equity money in 1986 from five banks and the construction firms that had won the licence to make a tunnel under the Channel.
The 225-strong banking syndicate that currently carries the Eurotunnel debts may have to wait even longer for their money than they originally negotiated.
But in the case of default they have a key asset to seize -- a train tunnel under the Channel which is attracting more and more users and has a licence for about a century.
